newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr survives scare as RBA misinterpreted.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr survives scare as RBA misinterpreted.

text.p: The Australian dollar survived a scare on Tuesday when a news report suggested the Reserve Bank of Australia had said interest rates would be cut again, but it was still looking heavy and the bias was for further losses.

The report, which turned out to be a misinterpretation, sent the dollar to its lowest levels in a week. However, even after the report was discounted the dollar remained under pressure, as the market judged that the RBA still held an easing bias.
At 4.30 p.m. the dollar stood at US$0.7373/78, down on an early US$0.7381/86 and a Monday close of US$0.7423/28. It had traded a US$0.7369/86 range through the day.

The RBA released its quarterly report on the economy and financial markets during afternoon trading. A wire service report said that RBA had said that rates could be eased again, but the item was based on the RBA's reasoning for the rate cuts in May and July, and was not an outlook for rates.

"Just seeing something like that come up without stating that it's talking about the last couple of rate cuts, not the next couple, may have affected the dollar a little bit," Commonwealth Bank chief economist Bruce Freeland said.
The RBA did say current rate settings could accomodate stronger growth in the short term without threatening inflation.

The outlook for inflation remained positive, with the RBA saying the key underlying rate would remain below two percent possibly into 1998, with domestic sources of inflation appearing to be in check.

As well, the RBA said the dollar was not a threat to inflation, because despite the fact that the dollar had fallen from around SU$0.80 in March to its current level, it had held up well in trade-weighted terms.
"If the exchange rate remains at current levels, it would imply relative stability in prices for imported consumer goods," the RBA said.

While traders remained wary of another cut in interest rates, which left the dollar under pressure, analysts said with the RBA expecting stronger growth there was no reason to expect a move any time soon.

"Another rate cut certainly is still possible, and the good news on inflation may still make it possible, but I'd still see unchanged rates as the most likely outcome, and remaining unchanged for quite a long time," Freeland said.
Treasurer Peter Costello shares the RBA's optimism on the outlook for improving growth, telling reporters ahead of a cabinet meeting that the economy could grow above four percent.
"I think if we can kill the savings problem and if we can beat inflation, we should be looking at an economy that grows at four percent plus," he said in Melbourne.
The prospect of stronger growth is providing little comfort to the dollar as long as the shadow of a rate cut hangs over it.
Traders said the dollar was likely to remain in the lower half of the US$0.73/75 range it has held since early July, with sellers expected to cap the dollar under US$0.74.
"I would tend to think that people would like to sell any sort of rally to US$0.7390/7400," said one trader, adding that the U.S. FOMC was likely to have little impact on the market.
Economists and financial markets do not expect the FOMC to lift U.S. rates at its meeting later today, although U.S. rates are seen retaining a tightening bias.
However, just as the topside was capped, support above US$0.73 was expected to prove very solid, with the unit unlikely to make a rapid break either way over the next few days.

On the crosses, the dollar ended slightly easier at 58.4 in trade weighted terms, having held steady with Monday's close of 58.5 through the morning. Against the yen the dollar ended at 87.10.20, almost unchanged from an early 87.17/27 and a Monday close of 87.11/21. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
